title: The 4-20 mA loop
summary: Why process transmitters send currents and why the zero sits at 4 mA.

sections.heading: Current loops
sections.body: A transmitter regulates the current in a loop between 4 and 20 mA. Because the current is the same everywhere in the loop, cable length barely matters. 4 mA is the **live zero**: 0 mA can only mean a broken loop.

sections.heading: NE 43 bands
sections.body: Measurement and failure information are separated.

sections.body: Percent from a loop current in mA.

sections.heading: Common mistake
sections.body: Configuring the input as 0-20 mA for a 4-20 mA transmitter: 4 mA then reads as 20 % and the whole range is shifted.

sections.heading: Summary and troubleshooting note
sections.body:
4-20 mA gives noise immunity and a live zero; NE 43 defines failure currents below 3.6 and above 21 mA.

**Troubleshooting note:** A reading stuck at the bottom with a wire-break diagnostic means 0 mA in the loop: check the loop wiring and the transmitter supply.

checkpoint.question: What does 0 mA on a 4-20 mA input mean?
options: A broken loop or missing supply
checkpoint.explanation: The live zero makes 0 mA a fault indication.
